Be very careful when you say stored procedures will prevent SQL injection. If done correctly, they can. But they can be implemented poorly enough that they fix nothing.

The easiest way to break one is to have a single parameter for the stored procedure. Name that parameter WhereClause. Build the WHERE clause dynamically and place that string in the WhereClause parameter. You now have a broken stored procedure.

Use parameterized queries to prevent the issue. Don't rely on sanitized inputs. You can still use stored procedures; just make sure you treat them like parameterized queries.

Having been a developer for 24 years, and having been responsible for managing developers myself for a large percentage of that time, I can give you a few things to look at.

How good are you at telling a client no? If you are constantly giving clients what they ask for, instead of helping them find a way to accomplish what they need in a maintainable way, you might not be performing well.

How many releases have you had to back out? This is the number one sign of poor developers, in my opinion, not to mention quality assurance issues.

How many defects have you fixed that have been re-opened? If you have a lot of these, you probably need to improve.

How many projects are you a bottleneck for? If there are many, you likely need to improve. Your code should be easy enough for anyone to work on. If you are the only one who can work on a specific task, either the rest of the team is lacking or you are. Odds are it is you.

Do you find yourself arguing with quality assurance often? If so, you probably need to improve. Either you are consistently delivering buggy code, or they simply don't trust you. Either scenario is a bad sign.

Do you find yourself spending a lot of time in a code review explaining how you got something to work? If so, you probably need to improve. Code should generally be self-explanatory, and during code reviews, you should not receive many questions—mostly head nods. Code isn't done until it is simple. Adding dependency injection to your code doesn't make you exceptional. Knowing when to and when not to add dependency injection to your code makes you exceptional.

For a single rail, I measure the distance from the ball to the rail and then aim at a spot that far behind the rail, using center ball and a medium speed.

For a long single rail, I apply a touch of inside (running English) and shoot a bit harder than pocket speed.

For a two rail kick, I typically use good speed with lots of inside English.

For a three rail kick, I apply a lot of top inside with pocket speed. As the cue ball moves up the table (closer to the point on the rail I am aiming for), the top spin drops to the middle and then down to low, while the inside spin turns to center and then adds a touch of outside.

So it really depends on the type of kick you are executing.

I had a chance to tell a chemistry teacher how I organized a class-wide scheme for the final exam.

The teacher allowed us to view the test the day before, but we couldn’t take notes—just a chance to see what we needed to study. We knew in advance this would happen, maybe a day early. So I gathered the class, and we divided the test among everyone. One student got questions one and two, another got two and three, a third got three and four, etc. Instead of trying to figure out the whole test, we just memorized the two questions we were assigned and wrote them down as soon as we could. Every question had two people covering it, so we had some error correction involved. Plus, we had one person with a near-photographic memory who was able to double-check everyone.

Once we coordinated and recreated the entire test, I and a few other top students completed the test open book style. We then compared answers and agreed on the correct ones. We distributed the answers with the instruction that everyone should randomly miss a few.

I took it a step further... because why not. The teacher allowed us to use portable music players during the test. She had previously caught a student who had taped notes on blank tapes, so the one rule was that we could only listen to commercially produced albums. Well, a local store had a bargain bin with inexpensive tapes. So I bought a copy of a classic album, covered the holes that prevent recording, and recorded the answers to the test.

She was pretty cool, and I ran into her after I graduated. She asked how everyone had done so well on that test. I explained what we did so she could close those loopholes. She found it both hilarious and mortifying. She did give me a hard time about how much effort we put into it, considering I was carrying a high average into the final without cheating. I told her it was more about figuring out if it would actually work than anything else. 😜
